uncited: Primitive Representation defines the geometric and photometric data structures used to approximate a 3D scene in Gaussian Splatting methods.
It solves the problem of representing continuous geometry and appearance with discrete, differentiable primitives that can be efficiently rasterized.

It sets itself apart from parent methods by explicitly defining the kernel shape (e.g., isotropic, half-space, or hybrid Bézier) and the associated attribute storage (e.g., opacity, normals, control points) that determine how light interacts with the primitive during rendering.
All child methods share the core requirement of defining a 3D primitive with a position, orientation, scale, and appearance attributes.
Parameterized as $\Sigma^w = R S S^T R^T$ in world space, where $R$ is rotation and $S$ is scaling.
The rendering pipeline projects these 3D primitives to 2D screen space.
The covariance transforms via the view matrix $W$ and projection Jacobian $J$: $\Sigma = J W \Sigma^w W^T J^T$.
The integral of the 3D density along the view direction yields the 2D splat density.
This variant represents primitives as planar disks with normal vectors, often used for surface extraction or meshing, differing from volumetric Gaussians by enforcing zero thickness.

Subsequent variants like 3D-HGS and BG-Triangle emerged to address specific limitations such as Gibbs phenomena at boundaries and aliasing, expanding the primitive representation beyond the standard isotropic Gaussian.
